summary:
Police-reported hate crime in Newfoundland and Labrador ran at 5.3 per 100,000 in 2024, the joint-lowest provincial rate in the country alongside Manitoba. The figure rests on 29 incidents, up from 19 in 2023. At those volumes the 51 per cent increase is statistically fragile, and police counts record only incidents that were reported to police.

The province has not required surgery to change a gender marker since an amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 that received Royal Assent on 13 April 2016. That amendment followed a December 2015 ruling by a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission on complaints brought by two trans women, and brought provincial law into line with the ruling.

A 2021 amendment extended change of sex designation to people who were not born in the province but have lived there at least three months. The resulting change certificate costs $25, counts as official provincial identification, and can be used by the holder to update records in other jurisdictions; for people born outside the country it serves as the identification document. The 2021 change followed earlier amendments that put a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates.

The province states that it cannot guarantee a birth certificate carrying an X gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations, a caveat that matters for anyone relying on provincial documents after leaving Newfoundland and Labrador.

Gender identity is a prohibited ground of discrimination under the province's human rights legislation, covering employment, housing and public and private accommodations.
tangentialFactors:
The provincial hate-crime rate sits below the national rate of 12.1 per 100,000 recorded for 2024 and below the highest provincial rate, Ontario's 16.0 per 100,000. Newfoundland and Labrador's 5.3 per 100,000 is tied with Manitoba for the lowest in the country.

Provincial comparisons of this kind are meaningful by rate rather than by count. Raw incident counts track population size, so a province recording more incidents is not thereby more dangerous; the 5.3 per 100,000 rate places Newfoundland and Labrador at the low end irrespective of its small absolute numbers.
localsOnly:
Applications to change sex designation in Newfoundland and Labrador are open to people aged 16 and over. Applicants under 16 are represented by a parent or legal guardian, with the consent of the other parent or guardian and the written consent of the applicant where they are between 12 and 15. Applicants must have been born in the province or have resided there at least three months.

The change application itself carries no fee. Charges apply only to official copies of updated documents: a new birth certificate costs $35, or $30 when ordered online.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been legal in the province since 2002.
outOfScopeNotes:
The provincial hate-crime rate is a total across all hate-crime categories. The inventory does not disaggregate it by targeted group, so no trans-specific provincial rate is sourced, and the 5.3 per 100,000 figure should not be read as a measure of risk to trans people specifically.

Egale Canada's 2024 analysis of police-reported hate crime, which covers offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity, is national in scope and provides no provincial breakdown.

Whether a provincial birth certificate carrying an X gender marker is accepted by authorities elsewhere is unresolved: the province declines to guarantee acceptance, and no independent assessment of acceptance rates is sourced.
